name: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery
summary: The largest branch of the vertebral artery. It takes a tortuous course between the medulla and the cerebellum, supplying the dorsolateral medulla, the inferior surface of the cerebellar hemisphere and vermis, the cerebellar tonsil and the choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle. Its occlusion (or, more often, occlusion of the parent vertebral artery) produces the lateral medullary syndrome, and a large cerebellar infarct in its territory can swell and compress the brainstem.

anatomy.location: Arises from the intracranial vertebral artery 1–2 cm below the vertebrobasilar junction, loops caudally around the medulla between the rootlets of the glossopharyngeal, vagus and accessory nerves, curves over the cerebellar tonsil (the caudal loop) and then ascends onto the inferior cerebellar surface.

subdivisions.name: Anterior and lateral medullary segments
subdivisions.note: perforators to the dorsolateral medulla: spinothalamic tract, spinal trigeminal nucleus, nucleus ambiguus, vestibular nuclei

subdivisions.name: Tonsillomedullary and telovelotonsillar segments
subdivisions.note: cerebellar tonsil, choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle

subdivisions.name: Cortical segment
subdivisions.note: inferior vermis and inferior hemispheric surface

function: Supplies the dorsolateral medulla and the inferior cerebellum (posterior lobe inferior surface, tonsil, inferior vermis) plus the fourth ventricular choroid plexus.

bestView.label: PICA loop beside the medulla and tonsil

imaging.normalAppearance: A small tortuous flow void beside the medulla on axial T2, seen more consistently on CTA/MRA as a loop around the tonsil. Its cerebellar territory is the inferior and posterior hemispheric surface below the horizontal fissure.

pathology.finding: Restricted diffusion in the dorsolateral medulla at the level of the inferior olive, sometimes extending to the inferior cerebellum; CT is usually normal.
pathology.pitfalls: Lesions are small: use thin-slice DWI and look on coronal reformats; a normal DWI in the first hours does not exclude it

pathology.pathology: PICA cerebellar infarct with mass effect
pathology.finding: Hypodensity of the inferior cerebellar hemisphere; over 2–4 days swelling compresses the fourth ventricle causing obstructive hydrocephalus and tonsillar descent.
pathology.timing: Maximal swelling day 2–4; monitor closely for hydrocephalus

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: DWI with thin slices; CTA of the vertebral arteries; repeat CT if drowsiness develops after a cerebellar infarct

lesionEffects.deficit: Loss of pain and temperature on the face with loss on the opposite body
lesionEffects.mechanism: Spinal trigeminal tract ipsilaterally and the already-crossed spinothalamic tract
Descending sympathetic fibers in the lateral medulla

examination: Pin-prick on the face compared with the trunk and limbs on each side
Palatal elevation, voice quality and swallowing
Finger-nose, heel-shin and gait; observe nystagmus direction
pearls: Crossed pain and temperature loss (face one side, body the other) with no weakness is the lateral medulla
Most Wallenberg strokes are from vertebral artery occlusion or dissection rather than PICA itself
A drowsy patient two days after a cerebellar infarct needs an urgent CT for hydrocephalus
